There the black Slave-ship swims, Freighted with human forms, Whose fettered, fleshless limbs Are not the sport of storms. In Ocean's vast domains,
Half-buried in the sand,
Lie skeletons in chains,
With shackled foot and hand.

Beyond the fall of dew,
Deeper than plummet lies,
Float ships with all their crew,
No more to sink or rise.

There glides the black Slave-ship,
Freighted with human forms,
Whose fettered, fleshless limbs
No longer fear the storms.

These are the bones of Slaves;
They gleam up from the deep;
They cry from yawning waves,
"We are the Witnesses that weep!"

Within Earth's boundless reach
Are markets for men's lives;
Their necks with chains are galled,
Their wrists are bound with gyves.

Dead bodies left to lie
Where kites their carrion seek;
Murders that terrify
And still the schoolboy's shriek!

All evil thoughts and deeds—
Anger, and lust, and pride—
The foulest, rankest weeds
That choke Life's groaning tide!

These are the griefs of Slaves;
They glare up from the deep;
They cry from unmarked graves,
"We are the Witnesses that weep!"

---

Beneath the ocean's vast expanse, half-hidden in the shifting sand, rest skeletal remains bound in chains, feet and hands still fettered. Deeper than any anchor could reach, past where dewdrops ever fall, sunken vessels drift with their crews, forever suspended between rising and sinking. There glides the dark slave-ship, laden with human cargo—limbs stripped of flesh yet still shackled, no longer troubled by ocean storms.

These skeletal remains belonged to enslaved people; they shimmer faintly from the depths below. From the gaping waters they cry out: "We stand as evidence!"

Across the broad reaches of the earth exist places where human beings are bought and sold; their throats bear the marks of iron collars, their wrists bent and bruised by shackles. Corpses left for vultures to devour in barren wastelands; killings so horrific they frighten children away from their games!

Every corrupt thought and vile action; wrath, desire, and arrogance; the most rotten, poisonous growths that strangle the flow of life itself!

These represent the suffering of enslaved people; they blaze forth from the depths. From graves unknown to any living soul, they proclaim: "We stand as evidence!"
outputs.L3:
# The Silent Testimony of the Deep

Beneath the vast, indifferent waves of the ocean lie the skeletal remains of countless enslaved people—bodies once bound by iron chains, now bound instead by sand and silence. These are the forgotten dead, those who did not survive the brutal crossing, whose lives ended not on distant shores but in the crushing depths of the sea itself. They are the remnants of a trade that treated human beings as cargo, and the ocean floor became their unmarked, unwilling tomb.

Scattered across that same ocean floor rest the wrecks of slave ships—vessels that once carried human cargo across the water, now themselves imprisoned by time and tide. Within their broken hulls remain the fettered bones of those who never reached land, never tasted freedom, and never received a proper burial. These ships will not rise again, and neither will the remains they carry. They are sealed away, permanent fixtures of a maritime graveyard that most of the world chooses not to see.

And yet, though hidden from human sight, these bones are not silent. They cry out from the depths—not with voices, but with the undeniable weight of their existence. They serve as witnesses, testifying across centuries to the horrors inflicted upon them: the chains, the suffering, the stolen lives, the profound injustice of being treated as property rather than people. Their testimony persists even where no living voice remains to speak it.

The horror, however, was not confined to the sea. On land, the machinery of slavery ground human beings into commodities—bought, sold, and traded in open markets as though they were livestock rather than people with families, histories, and futures. Their bodies bore the physical evidence of this system: scars left by chains, wounds left by shackles, marks that spoke of cruelty inflicted again and again. Communities lived under constant threat, terrorized by violence and the ever-present specter of murder, as human life was devalued and discarded with impunity.

This entire system was built upon and sustained by profound moral corruption. Anger, lust, pride, and evil deeds intertwined to create a machinery of oppression that choked the very flow of life—stifling not only the bodies of the enslaved but the moral conscience of the societies that permitted such atrocities to flourish. And just as the bones beneath the ocean cry out as witnesses, so too do the unknown, unmarked graves of enslaved people on land. Scattered and forgotten, these graves nonetheless testify to the injustices committed, refusing to let the truth remain buried along with the dead.

Together, the drowned and the buried form a chorus of silent witnesses—testimony written not in words, but in bones, in scars, in the earth and sea themselves—demanding that the horrors of slavery never be forgotten, and that justice, however delayed, remain a debt still owed to the dead.
outputs.L4:
# The Depths That Remember

The poem opens with a descent—not merely into water, but into history's most shameful depths. The imagery is unflinching: sunken slave ships lie scattered across ocean floors, their hulls become tombs, their cargo holds transformed into underwater graveyards. Here, beneath waves that show no scars, rest the skeletal remains of countless enslaved people who never survived the Middle Passage. Chains that once bound living flesh now rest against bone, rusted but unbroken, testament to a bondage that pursued its victims even into death.

The poet does not allow these images to remain distant or abstract. Instead, a deliberate and haunting parallel emerges between the ocean's hidden horrors and slavery's visible cruelties on land. Just as bodies lay chained beneath the sea, so too were bodies chained in plantation fields, in slave markets, in the holds of ships that did complete their crossings. Murder was not confined to shipwrecks and drownings—it continued on shore, in whippings, in the casual violence of an economic system built on human suffering. The poem suggests that the moral corruption enabling such atrocities did not drown with the ships that sank; it survived and thrived, embedding itself into the fabric of societies that profited from human bondage.

Central to the poem's power is its treatment of memory and witness. The submerged bones, resting in unmarked and unknown graves, become more than mere remains—they transform into eternal witnesses. Though no human eye may ever locate these underwater graveyards, though no ceremony marks their resting places, the poem insists that this absence of recognition does not equal erasure. Rather, these bones cry out silently but persistently, their very existence a testimony that refuses to be silenced by time, tide, or willful forgetting.

This act of bearing witness carries profound moral weight. The poem argues that slavery's guilt is not something that can be washed away by the passing centuries or buried by comfortable historical distance. The ocean itself becomes complicit in this refusal to forget—its depths preserve rather than erase, its currents circulate rather than dissolve the evidence of atrocity. In this way, the natural world becomes an unwilling but permanent archive of human cruelty.

Ultimately, the poem functions as both elegy and indictment. It mourns the countless unnamed dead while simultaneously refusing to let their deaths be rendered meaningless or forgotten. The demand embedded in every line is clear: this history must never be denied, minimized, or allowed to fade from collective consciousness. The bones beneath the waves, though invisible to living eyes, remain eternally present in their moral claim upon the living—a haunting reminder that some debts of memory and justice can never be fully settled, only acknowledged and carried forward.
outputs.L5:
# The Ocean's Half-Truth

There's an old saying that the ocean never lies, but perhaps that's only half true. The sea speaks in tides and currents, in the crash of waves against ancient rock, yet it withholds as much as it reveals. Beneath its shimmering surface, the ocean keeps secrets—shipwrecks swallowed whole, creatures that have never seen light, mountain ranges deeper than any on land.

To stand at the shore is to witness only half the story. The half we see is beautiful: sunlight dancing on waves, the rhythmic pull of tides, gulls wheeling overhead. But this is merely the ocean's public face, the lie of simplicity it tells to those who never venture beneath.

The other half—the truth—exists in darkness and pressure, in ecosystems that operate by rules foreign to our sunlit world. Scientists estimate we've explored less than twenty percent of our oceans. We know more about the surface of Mars than the depths of our own seas.

Perhaps this is the ocean's greatest lie: convincing us we understand it through a glimpse of its surface. We see half of what exists—half the creatures, half the currents, half the story—and mistake this fraction for the whole truth.

The ocean doesn't lie maliciously. It simply exists in dimensions we cannot easily access, keeping its depths as a kind of honest secret. What looks like deception is really just vastness—a reminder that some truths require us to dive deeper, to look beyond the comfortable half we think we know, before we can claim to understand anything at all.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write or recall a poem in the style of Longfellow's antislavery verse, using imagery of drowned slave ships, chains, and the ocean as witnesses to human suffering.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Ocean's Testimony

The sea keeps count of all its dead,
Though waves erase what tongues have said,
And in its depths, where sunlight fails,
Lie broken hulls of slaver's sails.

The anchor chains still bind the bone
Of those who crossed but ne'er came home—
Not free, nor bound, but lost between
Two shores that neither claimed nor seen.

O Ocean, ancient, deep, and vast,
You hold the record of the past,
The manifests no hand did write,
The screams that pierced the tropic night.

The captain's log records the "cargo lost,"
So many souls, so little cost—
As if a life could be a sum,
As if a heart could beat then come

To nothing but a column's tare,
A weight subtracted, unaware
That every drop of ocean brine
Remembers what was thrown as fine.

Beneath the coral, bleached and white,
Where fish now dart in dappled light,
The iron cuffs still hold their grip
On wrists that fell from sinking ship.

No monument of marble stands
To mark this grave in fathomed sands,
Yet every tide that meets the shore
Whispers what was done before.

The moon, indifferent, pulls the tide
Across the graves spread far and wide,
As if to say: *I saw it all,
The chains, the whip, the bodies' fall.*

And still the merchant ships set sail,
And still the profit does not fail
To blind the eyes that will not see
The chains that bind humanity.

O Reader, when you walk the shore
And hear the waves' eternal roar,
Know that beneath that endless blue
Lie those who once were men like you—

Who laughed, who loved, who hoped, who feared,
Whose names no living lips have cheered,
Whose only mourners are the waves
That rock them still in ocean graves.

Let not the sea's vast silence be
Mistaken for complicity—
It speaks in every crashing wave:
*Remember those I could not save.*

---

*In the tradition of Longfellow's "The Slave's Dream" and "The Witnesses," this poem seeks to honor those lost in the Middle Passage, using the ocean as both grave and unwilling witness to history's cruelty.*
